source: Shepard, Hovland & Jenkins (1961) Learning and memorization of classifications [described in Lian et al. 2024]
finding: Six category structures on 8 stimuli (3 binary dimensions: size, colour, form), 4 per category. Type I: one diagnostic dimension. II: XOR on two dimensions. III and V: rule plus exception. IV: family resemblance. VI: arbitrary (memorise all). Difficulty runs roughly I < II < III,IV,V < VI. Authors concluded people abstract dimensions, then test rules.
numbers: 8 stimuli, 3 binary dims, 6 types.
limits: Known only second hand from papers opened this session. Original not read.
agent_relevance: The six types are a ready bank of problem classes: one-feature rule, XOR, rule+exception, prototype-like, arbitrary. A template for an S0 gate that labels a task by structure.

source: Smith, Minda & Washburn (2004) replication of Shepard 1961 [described in Lian et al. 2024]
finding: Replication with all 6 stimulus permutations per type (36 tasks). Each human did 6 tasks, 24 blocks of all 8 stimuli = 192 trials per task. Used as the human benchmark by later model papers.
numbers: 36 tasks, 24 blocks x 8 stimuli; accuracies reported for odd blocks 1,3,...,23.
limits: Second hand via Lian et al. 2024.
agent_relevance: Robustness trick: permute which stimuli map to which category. For agent evals, permute surface labels the same way.

source: Medin & Schaffer (1978) Context theory of classification learning [described in Lian et al. 2024]
finding: Introduced the exemplar (context) model. Two sets of 16 stimuli on four binary dimensions (colour, form, size, number). Train on 9 items with feedback (5 category A, 4 B), then after an interpolated task classify all 16 with no feedback. Stimulus 7 (a training item far from the prototype) versus Stimulus 4 (closer to the prototype) separate exemplar from prototype predictions.
numbers: 9 training items, 7 transfer items, 4 binary dims.
limits: Second hand. Original per-item numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Pick probe items where the two theories disagree. An agent probe for rule versus similarity should do the same.

source: Lian, Varma & MacLellan (2024) Cobweb: an incremental and hierarchical model of human-like category learning
finding: Cobweb (category-utility tree) fits Medin & Schaffer 1978 data and behaves partly like a prototype model, partly like an exemplar model, depending on the tree level used for prediction.
numbers: Medin-Schaffer: correlation with human 0.768 (leaf level), 0.713 (basic level); RMSD 0.166 and 0.130. Stimulus 7 vs 4 prob: leaf 0.750 vs 0.735; basic 0.826 vs 0.837. 200 predictions per stimulus (40 seeds x 5).
limits: Quote: Cobweb 'does not rigidly adhere to prototype- or exemplar-like behavior'. Simulation, no new human data.
agent_relevance: Supports a hybrid: one store read at different granularity. Fits a memory that keeps both cases and summaries.

source: Lian et al. (2024) Cobweb on Shepard Types I-VI vs Smith et al. 2004 human curves
finding: Cobweb learning curves track human curves for most Shepard types but fail on Type VI (arbitrary) at basic level and are weaker on Type III.
numbers: Correlation, basic level: I 0.981, II 0.929 (leaf 0.932), IV 0.910, V 0.984 (both levels), VI -0.375 (leaf 0.884). RMSD 0.075-0.231. Leaf level hits 100% on Type I after block 1.
limits: Fit uses 12 odd blocks only. Type III value unclear in the extracted table. Leaf predictions too deterministic.
agent_relevance: Even good models miss the arbitrary case. For arbitrary tasks a rule-seeking agent should stop hunting rules and memorise.

source: Fific, Little & Nosofsky (2010) Logical-rule models of classification response times, Psychological Review 117
finding: Formalises rule-based classification as independent decisions on each dimension (random walks) combined by logical rules (serial or parallel, self-terminating or exhaustive). Tested against the exemplar-based random-walk model (EBRW) on response times.
numbers: Experiment 1: 5 subjects, many sessions, instructed disjunctive rule. Serial self-terminating model best BIC for Subjects 2,3,4,5; parallel self-terminating best for Subject 1. Parallel-exhaustive, serial-exhaustive, coactive and EBRW gave 'quite poor fits' for all subjects.
limits: Small N, highly separable dimensions, explicit rule instructions. Nosofsky is an exemplar theorist and still finds rule use here.
agent_relevance: Rules are real when dimensions are separable and the rule is known. Expect rule use in clean separable tasks, similarity in messy ones.

source: Fific et al. (2010) introduction: three families of category models
finding: Early work assumed categories are sets of logical rules. Exemplar models (Medin & Schaffer 1978; Nosofsky 1986) then dominated. Decision-bound models (Ashby & Townsend 1986) divide a perceptual space with boundaries.
numbers: Three families: rules, exemplars, decision bounds.
limits: Intro summary only.
agent_relevance: A three-way map (rule, similarity, boundary) usable as S0 class labels.

source: Ashby & Rosedahl (2017) A neural interpretation of exemplar theory, Psychological Review 124
finding: Exemplar theory: the chance of choosing category A rises with summed similarity to all stored exemplars. The authors give a striatal-learning version (cortical-striatal synapse plasticity) with identical quantitative predictions that also explains phenomena the cognitive version cannot.
numbers: Claims exemplar theory has been 'the most prominent cognitive theory of categorization for more than 30 years'.
limits: Theory paper. Exemplar fits mostly accuracy data.
agent_relevance: Two systems: explicit rule search and slow implicit similarity learning. An agent needs both modes and a way to switch.

source: Ashby & Rosedahl (2017) on rule-based versus information-integration tasks
finding: Information-integration (II) tasks have no verbalisable rule; rule-based (RB) tasks do. RB learning is explicit; II learning is procedural and sensitive to feedback timing (II hurt when feedback is delayed). Some amnesic patients learn categories without remembering the session, a problem for pure exemplar-memory accounts.
numbers: Qualitative; no single N. Feedback delay example: 500 ms.
limits: Argument paper; evidence cited from other work.
agent_relevance: If no short rule exists, searching for one wastes steps. The gate should detect 'no short rule' and fall back to case retrieval.

source: Jagadish, Binz, Saanum, Wang & Schulz (2024) Human-like category learning by injecting ecological priors from LLMs into neural networks
finding: An LLM (Claude-v2) generated about 10,000 category-learning tasks; a transformer meta-learned on them (ERMI) predicts human choices better than seven other models.
numbers: Badham et al. 2017 data (Shepard types 1-4 replication): posterior model frequency ERMI 0.43+-0.05, RMC 0.41+-0.05, MI 0.10, PFN 0.05; GCM, prototype, Rule, Rulex each <=1%. BIC: ERMI 38722.13 vs Claude-v2 prompted as a participant 39816.90.
limits: Classic models lose mainly through the parameter penalty in BIC; log-likelihood GCM 177.35, PM 201.19 vs ERMI 200.82 (fit well).
agent_relevance: A prompted LLM is a worse human-like learner on categories than a model with the right priors. A scaffold may supply such priors.

source: Jagadish et al. (2024) Shepard types: difficulty order for humans, ERMI, plain LLM
finding: ERMI reproduces the human difficulty order on Shepard's six types. A plain meta-learner (MI) and Claude-v2 do not. Claude-v2 as a direct learner reaches zero error on most levels in about 3 blocks, finds Type 2 harder than 3-5, but the order does not match humans.
numbers: MSE to human curves (Table 5): ERMI 0.0287, MI 0.2627, PFN 0.1736, RMC 0.1003. Claude-v2 MSE 0.18 vs ERMI 0.05 (Badham data). Decay coefficient ERMI 1.24 vs human 0.44 (learns faster). MI finds Type 2 as hard as Type 6.
limits: One LLM (Claude-v2), prompted. Simulated 50 runs per type.
agent_relevance: LLMs learn rules too fast and in the wrong difficulty order. Do not trust an LLM's own sense of which class is hard.

source: Jagadish et al. (2024) Smith & Minda 1998 and Devraj et al. 2021: prototype early, exemplar later
finding: Humans are better fit by a prototype model in the first five blocks and by an exemplar model later (Smith & Minda 1998). ERMI shows the same drift; plain MI does not; Claude-v2 is fully exemplar-based from block 2.
numbers: Task: 14 six-dimension stimuli, blocks of 56 trials. ERMI drift slope -0.01+-0.004, z=-2.54, p<0.01; MI -0.002+-0.005, z=-0.47, p=0.63. Devraj et al. replication: ERMI posterior frequency 0.32; BIC ERMI 41207.20 vs Claude-v2 42401.42.
limits: ERMI is exemplar-based from block 2, earlier than humans.
agent_relevance: Early learning: summarise. Later: store cases. An agent memory could follow the same schedule.

source: Jagadish et al. (2024) Johansen & Palmeri (2002) transfer generalisation
finding: 9 four-dimension training stimuli, 7 transfer stimuli T1-T7 without feedback. Humans assign T5-T7 mostly to A and T1-T4 mostly to B. ERMI mostly matches that pattern.
numbers: Humans: T5,T6,T7 mostly A; T1-T4 mostly B. ERMI: T1,T3,T4 more B; T5-T7 more A.
limits: T2 resembles the prototype on some dimensions; ERMI and humans differ there.
agent_relevance: Transfer items reveal whether a learner used a rule or similarity. Use them as probe questions.

source: Jagadish, Thalmann, Coda-Forno, Binz & Schulz (2026) Meta-learning ecological priors from LLMs explains human learning and decision making (v3)
finding: Extends ERMI to 15 experiments across function learning, category learning and decision making; beats established cognitive models in trial-by-trial prediction.
numbers: 15 experiments; about 10,000 LLM-generated category tasks.
limits: Preprint. Its text says strategy moves from exemplar to prototype, which is the reverse of the 2024 paper and data (prototype early, exemplar late).
agent_relevance: Even the authors state the time direction inconsistently. Check original data before relying on the order.

source: Russin, Pavlick & Frank (2025) The dynamic interplay between in-context and in-weight learning in humans and neural networks
finding: Networks with in-context learning (ICL) plus in-weight learning (IWL) reproduce a human curriculum effect: blocked training helps when a category has a simple rule; interleaved helps when it does not.
numbers: Human effect (from earlier study): interaction p=0.04; blocking advantage d=0.47 for rule-like, interleaving advantage d=0.33 for rotated. Task: 2 dims x 8 values = 64 items, 32 train (16 per category). IWL-only net: interleaving better in both conditions (p<10^-3), through catastrophic forgetting.
limits: Small meta-learned transformers, not full LLMs. Human numbers second hand.
agent_relevance: ICL does fast rule inference. For an agent with no weight updates, present examples of one rule together when a rule exists; mix them when it does not.

source: Russin et al. (2025) ICL fails on non-rule (rotated) categories
finding: On rule-like blocked trials ICL reaches near-perfect accuracy at once. On rotated tasks (no simple rule) ICL fails and in-weight learning takes over, which causes forgetting if trials are blocked.
numbers: Rotation of axes by 45 degrees; 32 learning items.
limits: Network simulations only; no test on large LLMs.
agent_relevance: In-context learning has a rule bias. For non-rule tasks give many varied cases.

source: Wikipedia: Concept learning
finding: Rule-based theories go back to if-then production systems; prototype theory is central tendency with graded typicality; exemplar theory is stored instances (GCM best known). Humans may use exemplars early and prototypes later (page's wording); multiple-prototype models sit in between.
numbers: Cites Rouder & Ratcliff 2006 and Goodman et al. 2008 for rule-based work; Anderson 1991, Love-Medin-Gureckis 2004, Vanpaemel & Storms 2008 for in-between models.
limits: Tertiary source, no numbers. Its order (exemplar early) contradicts the Smith & Minda data as reported in the ERMI 2024 paper.
agent_relevance: Use as a map only.

source: Rouder & Ratcliff (2006) Comparing exemplar- and rule-based theories of categorization, Current Directions in Psychological Science 15
finding: From a search summary only: predictions of the two theories often mimic each other; they can be told apart; the data support neither alone; authors suggest a developmental view in which categorisation starts with rules.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Abstract level only.
agent_relevance: Mimicry means one success tells little. An S0 gate should not fix the class from one outcome.

source: Rouder & Ratcliff (2004) Comparing categorization models, J Exp Psychol General 133
finding: From a search summary only: four experiments competitively test rule and exemplar models. The stimulus type changes which model wins.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened. The PMC link I tried was Ashby & Rosedahl 2017, not this paper.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: stimulus form decides rule versus exemplar. Relevant to task-type routing.

source: Goodman, Tenenbaum, Feldman & Griffiths (2008) A rational analysis of rule-based concept learning, Cognitive Science 32
finding: From a search summary only: Bayesian inference over a grammar of logical rules, prior favouring short rules, matches the best rule models with fewer free parameters, tested on two classic category-learning experiments.
numbers: No numbers read (PDF fetch failed).
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: A prior on short rules is the formal reason to try the shortest rule first.

source: Ellis (2023) Human-like few-shot learning via Bayesian reasoning over natural language
finding: An LLM proposes natural-language concept hypotheses, an LLM turns them into code to check, Bayes reweights them, and the prior is tuned on human ratings. Tested on the Number Game and logical concepts.
numbers: Number Game: tuned prior R^2=0.95 with 100 samples against human ratings (average of 8 people); 50-100 hypotheses suffice. Logical concepts: R^2=0.81 with 100 proposals, within 3% of human accuracy, more accurate than GPT-4 alone; GPT-4 judgments 'decidedly different from humans'. English hypotheses beat Python hypotheses.
limits: Human data from older studies; Codex and GPT-4 era; few raters.
agent_relevance: Hypotheses in words, check, then weight: a cheap rule-learning loop that beats raw prompting.

source: Tano, Romano, Sigman, Salles & Figueira (2019) Towards a more flexible Language of Thought: Bayesian grammar updates after each concept exposure
finding: Boolean concept experiment: people compile frequently used expressions into new symbols; learning times fit a Bayesian agent that updates its grammar. Restates the law that Boolean concept difficulty tracks the length of the shortest propositional program.
numbers: N and times not extracted.
limits: Read abstract and introduction only.
agent_relevance: Repeated rule patterns should become named operators in the schema, which speeds later problems.

source: Chari & Pattanaik (2026) Wild guesses and mild guesses in active concept learning
finding: LLM-proposed program hypotheses with Bayesian weights on the Number Game. Expected-information-gain queries win when falsification is needed but lose on simple concepts because proposals become invalid ('support-mismatch trap'). Positive Test Strategy keeps proposals valid and converges faster on simple rules.
numbers: No percentages extracted; qualitative across Number Game tasks.
limits: Preprint under review. Abstract and introduction only.
agent_relevance: For simple rules, test the best hypothesis first before hunting for the most informative counterexample.

source: Ashby & Rosedahl (2017): rule-exemplar hybrids RULEX, ATRIUM, COVIS
finding: RULEX (Nosofsky, Palmeri & McKinley 1994) builds conjunctive rules and stores exceptions; ATRIUM combines a rule module and an exemplar module; COVIS pairs an explicit rule system with a procedural learner.
numbers: Named models only.
limits: Names and roles only.
agent_relevance: Rule plus exception list is a natural agent memory format.

source: Jagadish et al. (2024) task statistics of LLM-generated category tasks
finding: LLM-written tasks match real classification datasets in noise, feature correlation and linearity. ERMI trained on them reaches state-of-the-art on OpenML-CC18.
numbers: About 10,000 generated tasks; most generated and real tasks favoured the linear model in a logistic vs polynomial comparison.
limits: No accuracy numbers read for OpenML-CC18.
agent_relevance: Real tasks are mostly near-linear: a one-feature or additive rule is a good first guess.

source: Fific et al. (2010) design choices that favour rules
finding: Stimuli had highly separable dimensions and subjects were given the rule explicitly; the authors chose this on purpose to favour rule use.
numbers: Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 (accuracy subjects A1, A2 instructed).
limits: With integral dimensions or no instructions the result could flip.
agent_relevance: Instructions change the strategy. Prompt wording may steer an LLM into a class.

source: Lian et al. (2024): Medin-Schaffer procedure note
finding: Learn nine items with feedback, do an interpolated task, then classify all 16 with no feedback. The delay is part of the design.
numbers: 9 train, 16 test.
agent_relevance: A delayed test is what separates summary memory from case memory.
